newsitem.title: USA: Clinton checks up on hurricane recovery effort.
newsitem.headline: Clinton checks up on hurricane recovery effort.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Saturday checked up on efforts to recover from Hurricane Fran and heard appeals for speedy federal assistance during a quick visit to a state he would like to steal from Republicans in the November 5 election.

North Carolina Governor Jim Hunt told Clinton the state had sustained $5-6 billion in damage from the September 5 storm and appealed to him to clear away bureaucratic red tape to get federal assistance to people quickly.
"Mr. President, this is the worst disaster this state has ever had," Hunt said at a roundtable discussion with Clinton and officials involved in the relief effort. "We need all the help that we can."

Clinton flew over some storm damage aboard his Marine One helicopter and said he was struck by the magnitude of the losses, particularly the number of homes without roofs. He also watched some videotape of the storm and its aftermath on the flight from Washington.

He told the roundtable discussion he was considering asking Congress for additional aid for North Carolina and other states hit by the storm before Congress takes an election-year recess on September 27.
"We'd like to know exactly what you need done. We want to do the best we can to fashion a relief package that is as adequate as possible within the limits of the law," he said.

The White House announced Clinton had awarded $5 million to begin repair work on highways and bridges. The Labour Department said it was providing an $8 million emergency grant to help workers who lost their jobs due to the storm destruction.

At least 39 people were killed by the storm, half of them in North Carolina. The state's agriculture losses are staggering, estimated at $616 million, with tobacco bearing the brunt of the losses, $185 million in crop damage.
Thousands of homes and businesses were destroyed or damaged along with many roads, bridges and other public property.

"I frankly was amazed when we flew over the damage at how much had been done to at least prepare the way to rebuild the homes and get the trees up and do the other things that have to be done ... We will do whatever we can to help," Clinton said.

Clinton was only in North Carolina for about three hours on what was considered an official trip, not a campaign visit, but it was long enough to get him some media publicity in a conservative state that is home to Elizabeth Dole, wife of Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole.

Dole holds a narrow lead in the public opinion polls in North Carolina. Clinton only lost the state by about 20,000 votes to Republican George Bush in 1992. Campaign officials said North Carolina was one of the keys to breaking the Republican stronghold in the South.

"It's like Florida, like Georgia -- states that Bob Dole is absolutely counting on to win," Clinton campaign spokesman Joe Lockhart said from Washington. "If we win one, two or three of them we can clearly unravel his strategy."
Clinton, wearing a casual shirt and khaki pants, also heard stories of heroism that took place during the crisis atmosphere spawned by the hurricane.

Tony Maupin risked his life by tying a garden hose around his waist and wading into rapid flood waters to reach a teenager clinging to a tree. He was able to save one teen but a second one was swept away and never found.
"Some people say I'm a hero," said Maupin, seated at Clinton's side. "I really don't think I'm a hero. I just consider myself a father, a husband, and hopefully a good neighbour."
